lead: On a long sight the horizontal line of sight rises away from the curved level surface, so the far staff reads too high; this is curvature. The air bends the ray slightly back towards the earth, so the staff reads a little lower; this is refraction. Curvature is the larger, so the combined correction is always subtracted from a long-sight reading. Where a long sight cannot be avoided, for example across a river or valley, reciprocal levelling cancels both errors, and the instrument's collimation error with them, by reading from both banks. Only a few syllabi list this topic by name, but every standard textbook covers it and it is a regular exam problem.
prereq: You need: the level line and horizontal line from Levelling terms and the collimation error of Levels and their adjustments.

sections.h3: Curvature, refraction and the combined correction

blocks.text: Let the instrument be at A and the staff at B, a horizontal distance d away, both on the same level surface. The horizontal line from A meets the staff at B at a height c above the level line. With R the earth's radius, (R + c)² = R² + d², and since c is tiny compared with 2R, c = d² ÷ 2R. With R = 6370 km, d in kilometres and c in metres:

C<sub>c</sub> = d² ÷ (2R) = 0.0785 d²   (subtract)
C<sub>r</sub> = (1/7) C<sub>c</sub> = 0.0112 d²   (add)
C = C<sub>c</sub> − C<sub>r</sub> = 0.0673 d²   (subtract)
blocks.where: d is the sight length in km; the corrections are in metres. The refraction factor 1/7 is an average for daytime conditions; it varies with temperature and pressure, which is why long sights near the ground at midday are unreliable.

blocks.text: At 100 m (d = 0.1 km) C is under 1 mm, which is why ordinary levelling ignores it. At 800 m it is 0.0673 × 0.64 = 0.043 m, far too large to ignore. Equal backsight and foresight lengths also cancel C, just as they cancel collimation error, because both readings are too high by the same amount. Rearranged, d = √(h ÷ 0.0673) = 3.855√h km gives the distance to the visible horizon from an eye h metres above the level surface.
Across a river the instrument cannot stand midway, so the sights cannot be balanced. Reciprocal levelling uses two set-ups instead:

items: Set the level very close to A (a few metres). Read the staff on A (a near reading, almost error-free) and on B (a far reading).
Take the level across and set it very close to B. Read B (near) and A (far).

Let h be the true fall from A to B and e the total error of a far reading (curvature − refraction + collimation). From near A: r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub> = h + e. From near B: r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub> = h − e.
Add and subtract the two equations.

blocks.text: h = ½[(r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub>) + (r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub>)];   e = ½[(r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub>) − (r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub>)]
blocks.where: r<sub>A</sub>, r<sub>B</sub>: readings with the level near A; r′<sub>A</sub>, r′<sub>B</sub>: readings with the level near B. h positive means A is higher than B. e minus 0.0673 d² gives the collimation error over the far sight.

blocks.text: The method assumes refraction is the same for both far sights. Taking the two sets at about the same time, ideally with two levels read at once, or averaging several sets, keeps that assumption reasonable.

examples.question: Reciprocal levelling across a river 800 m wide between A (RL 150.000 m) and B gave: level near A, staff on A 1.428 m and on B 2.365 m; level near B, staff on B 1.815 m and on A 0.980 m. Find the true difference of level, the RL of B, the combined correction for 800 m, and the collimation error of the level.
steps: From near A: r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub> = 2.365 − 1.428 = 0.937 m. From near B: r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub> = 1.815 − 0.980 = 0.835 m.
True difference h = ½(0.937 + 0.835) = 0.886 m; it is positive, so B is 0.886 m lower than A.
Error in one far reading e = ½(0.937 − 0.835) = 0.051 m.
Combined curvature and refraction for d = 0.8 km: C = 0.0673 × 0.8² = 0.043 m.
Collimation error over 800 m = 0.051 − 0.043 = 0.008 m (readings too high, so the line of sight points upward), an angle of 0.008 ÷ 800 × 206 265 ≈ 2″.
examples.answer: B is 0.886 m below A, so RL of B = 149.114 m. The far-sight error is 0.051 m, of which 0.043 m is curvature and refraction and 0.008 m (about 2″ upward) is collimation.

traps: Entering d in metres in 0.0673 d². For 800 m, d = 0.8 km and C = 0.043 m; with d = 800 the answer is 43 000 m.
Adding the combined correction. Curvature makes the far reading too large, so C is subtracted; only the refraction part on its own is additive.
Taking 0.0785 d² as the net correction. That is curvature alone; with refraction the net is 0.0673 d².
Mixing the order of subtraction in the two set-ups. Use (reading on B − reading on A) in both, or the two errors do not cancel.
Claiming reciprocal levelling removes refraction always. It cancels only the part that is the same for both far sights.

quiz.q: Give the curvature, refraction and combined corrections with their signs.
quiz.a: C<sub>c</sub> = 0.0785 d² (subtract), C<sub>r</sub> = 0.0112 d² (add), C = 0.0673 d² (subtract), with d in km and C in m.

quiz.q: Why does balancing backsight and foresight lengths remove curvature and refraction?
quiz.a: Both readings are too high by the same 0.0673 d², and the height difference uses BS − FS, so the equal errors cancel.

quiz.q: Find the combined correction for a sight of 1.5 km.
quiz.a: C = 0.0673 × 1.5² = 0.0673 × 2.25 = 0.151 m, subtracted from the reading.

quiz.q: A lighthouse lamp is 30 m above sea level. From how far away can an observer whose eye is 1.5 m above the sea just see it?
Near P: P 1.200 m, Q 2.000 m. Near Q: Q 1.950 m, P 1.350 m. Find the true difference and the far-sight error.
In the last question the river is 500 m wide. Is 0.100 m a reasonable far-sight error? What does it suggest?
quiz.a: C for 0.5 km is 0.0673 × 0.25 = 0.017 m, so 0.083 m is left: a large collimation error (about 34″) or a disturbed set-up. The instrument should be tested with the two-peg test.

beyond: Not for the exam. Precise river crossings use two levels read at the same moment, or a total station measuring reciprocal vertical angles, and the refraction coefficient is estimated from the observations instead of fixed at 1/7. The same curvature geometry sets the height of microwave and radio towers needed for line of sight. Search for refraction coefficient k, reciprocal trigonometric heighting and line-of-sight clearance.

figure.caption: Left: the far staff is read where the horizontal line meets it, above the level line by C = 0.0785 d²; refraction bends the ray down by about a seventh of that, so the net correction is 0.0673 d². Right: the two set-ups of the worked example, whose average cancels the far-sight error of 0.051 m.
